scenario: AITA for “cheating” my family out of hundreds of dollars? | I have a giant family. My mom and my dad both have a lot of siblings and they’re also both the youngest in their families. This means I’m nearly the youngest of over 20 cousins. We all live close so we throw gigantic family get togethers. All the time. My grandparents own a pretty big ranch just outside of town. They’re not rich by any means, but land is cheap out here and they’ve owned the property for a long time. Because these gatherings sometimes attract upwards of 40 people, their ranch has been the venue of choice for as long as I can remember. My uncles are all stereotypically masculine dudes, as are a lot of my older cousins, so our rendezvous generally revolve around sports, grilling, and gambling. Gambling isn’t exactly my cup of tea, but I participate for the sake of being social. I usually lose a fair bit of money because I don’t play cards or know sports teams as well as everybody else. It’s gotten to the point where it’s become a reoccurring joke amongst family members. Well this time around we have an especially large gathering. So large that It’s determined there’s too many people to coordinate our typical gambling games. To make things simpler, my aunt comes up with an idea. She fills a jar full of beans and places it high up on the mantle. She tells us it’s $20 a guess and whoever guesses closest to the number of beans inside gets to take home all the money. For whatever reason this new form of betting got everyone in an especially adversarial spirit. Almost all of the adults participated and many even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Remember how I’m typically ignorant when it comes to gambling? Well this time I was in my element. I could tell the jar was a typical 64oz mason jar, which a quick Google search told me was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Divide the jar by the beans and I got 773. Then I assumed 20% of it was air, which left me with ~619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and the other for 630. As I’m making my bet, people are giving me crap like “it’d be easier if you just gave it directly to me” and all the other usual ball busting, but I just smile and say nothing. Some can tell something’s up and continue to give me grief for the rest of the night. After probably 40 minutes of interrupted counting, my aunt informed everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anybody else’s. At first everybody was super happy for me, laughing about how lucky I am. One of the suspicious cousins from earlier asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately I could see people’s faces start to sour. One of my uncles said “that’s bullshit” and left the room. It ended up being nearly $1100. My parents tell me that I should offer to return it because I didn’t earn it fairly. I argue that I had all the same information as everybody else. AITA for keeping the money?

I’m used to making firm decisions, handling pressure quietly, and taking responsibility when things go wrong. Carrying that role over many years has shaped how I evaluate risks and make choices. Do you think long-term roles centered on protection and provision influence someone's overall decision-making style?

Absolutely. The long-term roles of **protection and provision**—especially when carried out consistently over years—do profoundly shape a person’s **decision-making style, risk tolerance, and even emotional responses**. Here’s how these roles might influence you (and others in similar positions), based on psychological, behavioral, and leadership research: --- ### **1. Decision-Making Style: The "Steady Hand" Approach** Your background likely fosters a **structured, proactive, and sometimes cautious** decision-making framework. Key traits this might cultivate: - **Long-Term Orientation**: You prioritize stability over short-term gains (e.g., saving for college vs. splurging on luxuries). This aligns with research on **"delayed gratification"** (Stanford marshmallow test) and the **"planning fallacy"** (underestimating long-term risks). - **Risk Aversion**: Protection instincts make you **prefer controlled risks** (e.g., diversified investments, insurance) over high-stakes gambles. Studies show that **families with dependents** tend to exhibit lower risk tolerance in financial decisions. - **Preemptive Problem-Solving**: You likely **anticipate challenges** (e.g., "What if my income drops?") and build buffers (emergency funds, side income). This mirrors **"preparatory coping"** in psychology—proactively addressing potential threats. - **Accountability as a Default**: Taking responsibility for mistakes reinforces a **"no-blame" culture** in your family, which can create a **high-trust environment** but may also lead to **over-apologizing** or **self-sacrifice** (a trait linked to "hyper-responsibility syndrome"). **Potential Blind Spots**: - **Over-reliance on control**: You might struggle with **uncertainty** (e.g., market crashes, health scares) because you’ve trained yourself to "fix" problems. This can lead to **analysis paralysis** or **avoidance of ambiguity**. - **Emotional suppression**: Quietly handling pressure may mean **deferring emotional needs** (yours or your family’s), which can strain relationships long-term. --- ### **2. Risk Assessment: The "Cost-Benefit Protector" Lens** Your risk evaluation is likely **filtered through a "family multiplier"**—meaning risks aren’t just personal but **multiplied by their impact on dependents**. This creates a unique framework: - **Financial Risks**: You might **overweight tail risks** (e.g., job loss, medical debt) because they could derail your family’s security. This aligns with **"loss aversion"** (Kahneman & Tversky), where losses feel 2–3x more painful than equivalent gains. - **Social/Emotional Risks**: You may **avoid situations** that could expose your family to instability (e.g., risky friendships, volatile relationships). Emotional and Psychological Traits** - **Resilience as a Shield**: Years of handling pressure likely built **emotional resilience**, but it may also create a **"stoic" facade**—suppressing vulnerability. This prevents burnout and models **work-life balance**. - **Outsource Emotional Labor**: Delegate **family emotional check-ins** to your partner or kids (e.g., "What’s one thing you’re proud of this week?"). This builds **shared responsibility**. - **Automate Stability**: Use tools like **robo-advisors, automatic savings**, or **family budget apps** to reduce cognitive load on "protection mode." - **Reframe "Enough"**: Ask: *"What’s the minimum viable security?"* (e.g., "Do we need a 6-month emergency fund, or 12?").
